fields.quote: Payment and notification now commit atomically
fields.rationale: The after function awaits db.transaction, then awaits publish. Contract: publish is an external operation outside the database transaction. Contract: a process can stop between awaited operations. Probe after.publish-before: paid true, notifications 0. Probe after.publish-after: paid true, notifications 1, then publish rejects. Probe after.concurrent: notifications 2. Those outcomes are not atomic commit of payment and notification. The same manifest later states that the change does not make them atomic.
Source title begins with Lantern Ledger: publish after the payment transaction.

fields.quote: A failed commit now prevents publication, while publication failure leaves a committed payment intact.
fields.rationale: After control flow invokes publish only after db.transaction fulfills. Probe after.commit: paid false, notifications 0. Probe before.commit: notifications 1. Probe after.publish-before and after.publish-after: paid true. Contract: callback or commit rejection rolls back staged writes, so after never reaches publish on those faults.
probe.mjs runs fixed named faults with no random input. probe-results.json assumptions: In-memory staged transaction and external notification counter; no actual database or process-kill simulation.

fields.quote: The supplied code has no durable outbox or delivery deduplication.
fields.rationale: Contract: Neither transaction nor publish supplies a delivery deduplication guarantee. Contract: No durable outbox, background retry, or cross-call lock is supplied. functions.mjs has only transaction, markPaid, and publish.
Section label. It does not assert a property of the code, contracts, or probes.
before() calls publish inside the transaction callback. Contract: transaction commits staged writes only after callback fulfillment. Probe before.none.events: begin, write, publish, commit.

fields.quote: The old callback marked the payment and published before the transaction committed. In the modeled commit failure, a notification escaped while the database write rolled back.
fields.rationale: before() awaits tx.markPaid(id) then publish(id) inside db.transaction. Probe before.commit: events begin, write, publish, rollback; paid false; notifications 1. Probe assert: a notification can escape before a failed commit.
Section label. It does not assert a property of the code, contracts, or probes.

fields.quote: Wait for the transaction to fulfill
fields.rationale: after() awaits db.transaction before publish. Contract: transaction fulfills with undefined after commit.

fields.quote: The changed function awaits the transaction before invoking publish. A write or commit rejection therefore prevents publication in that invocation.
fields.rationale: after() has await db.transaction(...) then await publish(id). A throw from write or commit rejects that await, so publish is not invoked in that call. Probe after.write and after.commit: notifications 0. The phrase in that invocation matches probe after.concurrent, which still publishes twice across two calls.
Section label. It does not assert a property of the code, contracts, or probes.

fields.quote: The database cannot roll back publication failures
fields.rationale: after() runs publish after the transaction has already fulfilled. Contract: publish is outside the database transaction. Probe after.publish-before and after.publish-after: paid remains true after publish rejects. There is no open transaction that can undo the committed payment or an external notification.

fields.quote: The author calls payment and notification atomic, but publish remains an external operation. Its rejection after commit leaves the payment recorded. It may also have delivered a notification before rejecting. The contract allows a process to stop between operations and supplies no durable retry. Concurrent invocations can each publish despite idempotent payment writes.
fields.rationale: Source body: The author says moving publish ... makes payment and notification atomic. Contract: publish is an external operation; rejection may happen before or after an externally visible notification. Probe after.publish-before: paid true, notifications 0. Probe after.publish-after: paid true, notifications 1. Contract: a process can stop between awaited operations; no durable outbox, background retry, or cross-call lock. Contract: markPaid is idempotent; neither transaction nor publish supplies delivery deduplication. Probe after.concurrent: notifications 2.
Section label. It does not assert a property of the code, contracts, or probes.

fields.quote: Commit first, with a remaining delivery gap
fields.rationale: Probe after.none.events: begin, write, commit, publish. Remaining gap: publish is after commit; contract allows a stop between awaited operations; after.publish-before leaves paid true with notifications 0; after.concurrent publishes twice.

fields.quote: The change prevents publication before a failed commit. It does not make the committed payment and the external notification atomic.
fields.rationale: Probe after.commit.notifications is 0; before.commit.notifications is 1. Non-atomicity: after.publish-before (paid without notification), after.publish-after (paid with notification then rejection), after.concurrent (two publishes), and the process-stop contract between commit and publish.

attribution_errors.quote: Payment and notification now commit atomically
attribution_errors.error: This headline states atomicity as a fact about the change. Source body attributes that claim to the author: The author says moving publish prevents notifications for failed commits and makes payment and notification atomic. /sections/2/content attributes the claim correctly. The title does not.

unresolved_uncertainty: Probe concurrent.paid is a single boolean, so two committed writes are not separately observed. The concurrent double-publish claim is taken from notifications 2 plus the idempotent-markPaid contract, not from a modeled second-row count.

Process stop between commit and publish is a contract statement. probe-results.json says there is no process-kill simulation. /sections/2/content attributes the stop to the contract, so this is unmodeled rather than contradicted.

Section eyebrows are labeled nonfactual as organizational text. If a later rubric treats every listed string as a claim, those four labels would need a different status, not a different evidence reading.
